entries.name: The Old Believers After 1815
entries.informalName: The Old Believers from Nicholas I to the toleration of 1905
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a study by a scholar who read the Russian sources. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906, the years after the earlier entry on the Old Believers. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: The main study is Conybeare's Russian Dissenters (1921). He read the Russian literature with care. He leans on Ivanovski, a writer for the Holy Synod who wrote against the Old Believers, and he says so. An English account of 1814 gives the picture at the start of these years. No Old Believer text of 1846 or 1905 was read. The statute of the Belaya Krinitsa hierarchy, the encyclical of 1862 and the text of the decree of 1905 are wanted.
entries.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here. The decree of 1905 says the Old Ritualists accept the sacraments and the doctrines of the Orthodox Church. They differ on points of ritual.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Old Believers after 1815. It carries on the earlier entry on the Old Believers. The entry on the Russian church under the Holy Synod tells the church they had left.
entries.why: Nicholas I tried to force the Old Believers into the state church. They found a bishop abroad in 1846 and built a hierarchy of their own. In 1905 the tsar gave them legal standing.
entries.teaser: Russia, 1815 to 1906. Old Believers under Nicholas I, a bishop found abroad in 1846, and the law of 1905.
entries.longDescription:
This entry carries the Old Believers on from 1815. By then the movement was split in two. The priestly branch took priests from the national church. The priestless branch had no priests at all, or priests of its own making.

Nicholas I pressed them hard. In 1827 a governor threatened to close the monastery of Nizhni-Voskresenski. The monks must join the state church, on terms Paul I had offered. That year the tsar also cut off the runaway priests who served the Rogozhskoe cemetery in Moscow and other places. The Popovtsy had long relied on those priests for the sacraments.

In 1832 the older laws that eased their lot were repealed. After that the Popovtsy could keep only priests who had joined them before 1826.

In 1854 the metropolitan Philaret made one chapel at the Rogozhskoe cemetery a church of the state church. In 1856 the old rites came back, with priests of Austrian ordination. The Popovtsy church was shut. Conybeare says its altars stayed sealed until 3 May 1883.

The priestly Old Believers wanted a bishop of their own. In 1844 the emperor Ferdinand let them bring one into his lands. He would sit at Belaya Krinitsa. Their agents searched the East. They found Ambrose, a Greek who had been metropolitan of Sarajevo. The Turks had expelled him from his see. He reached Belaya Krinitsa, in Austrian Bukovina, on 12 October 1846.

Ivanovski, a writer for the Holy Synod, says a monk who was there called the rite uncanonical. Conybeare passes this on with care. The Old Believers took Ambrose as their bishop all the same.

The new hierarchy grew fast. In 1849 a new bishop, Cyril, made Sophronius bishop of Simbirsk. Sophronius led the Russian Popovtsy. Within twelve years the church had ten sees across Russia. In 1861 it broke free of Belaya Krinitsa. From 1863 the state began to tolerate its priests.

Orthodox writers said the new bishops were not true bishops. So the priestly Old Believers asked the Patriarch of Constantinople to accept them, in 1875, 1892 and 1896. A commission there ruled for the bishop of Sarajevo in 1899. Conybeare calls this a quiet yes.

The priestless branch split over marriage. Conybeare says one group allowed it and the other did not, and each counted millions of souls.

On 17 April 1905 an imperial decree set the Old Ritualists apart from other dissenters. It let them form a church, with the rights of the Lutherans and Catholics. Their clergy no longer had to serve in the army.

On 25 August 1905 a synod of the priestly branch met. It ordered that the day of the decree be kept as a holy day for ever.
voices: Ambrose — the deposed metropolitan of Sarajevo whom the priestly Old Believers made their bishop at Belaya Krinitsa in 1846; his own words are not read here
Ivanovski — a writer for the Holy Synod against the Old Believers, whose account Conybeare uses and weighs
entries.legacy: The decree of 1905 gave the Old Believers rights they had long been denied. The priestly branch entered the new century with bishops of its own. The priestless branch brought its old arguments over marriage. Old Belief is still practiced today, as the evidence for this entry's living mark shows.
entries.peopleNote: No Old Believer of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: Old Belief is still practiced. The Moscow Metropolia of the Russian Orthodox Old-Rite Church runs an official site with news dated November 2026. entries.name: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, 1698 to 1815
entries.informalName: The union of the Romanians of Transylvania with Rome
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on the union's own acts. Its window runs from 1698 to 1815, from the union to the end of the era. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate to strong, and from inside the union. Nilles's edition of 1886 prints the union's own papers in Latin and Romanian. Its scan is badly damaged in places, and the quotes keep the damage. Bunea wrote his life of Bishop Klein (1900) for the 200th year of the union, and it too speaks for the union. Almost no Orthodox witness has been read. Visarion appears only through Bunea and the empress. The years from 1751 to 1815 are not told.
entries.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Romanian Greek Catholic Church from the union of 1698 to 1815. The next entry carries it on to 1906. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948. The Jesuits who began the talks are told in the entry on the Society of Jesus.
entries.why: On 7 October 1698 Romanian priests at Alba Iulia joined Rome. Jesuits had begun the talks. Orthodox Romanians pushed back. Bishop Klein pressed the court for his people's rights.
entries.teaser: Transylvania, 1698 to 1815. The union with Rome signed at Alba Iulia, the Jesuits who began it, the new seat at Blaj, and Bishop Klein.
entries.longDescription:
On 7 October 1698 Romanian clergy at Alba Iulia joined the Roman Catholic Church. The act is dated in Latin. It names the bishop, the archpriests and the priests of the Wallachian churches as its makers. Wallachian was the Latin word for Romanian.

The act asks for the same privileges that Roman Church priests have, under the emperor's decree. The Jesuit house history says an imperial letter of 1692 had given united priests of the Greek rite the rights of the Latin clergy. Nilles prints it.

The Jesuits of Alba Iulia opened the talks. The synod of 1701 says so. Its Latin says that the talks of union began through the work and skill of the Jesuit fathers living at Alba Iulia (opera ac solertia Patrum S. J., Albae-Juliae degentium). Nilles was himself a Jesuit. He adds that the house history shows the Jesuit fathers almost alone tending the Lord's vineyard at Alba Iulia in those years.

The state kept a hand on the church. In 1728 Charles VI ordered the united Romanian clergy to meet in an electoral synod and give him three candidates for the bishop's seat. The synod met at Alba Iulia on 4 June 1728. The Catholic bishop of Transylvania was there as the king's commissioner. So was the rector of the Jesuit college at Cluj, as the emperor's order required.

The bishop's seat moved to Blaj. Blaj was then only a Calvinist and Hungarian village. A contract with the court chamber, dated 31 August 1736, gave the estate of Blaj to the bishopric. The bishop took it in May 1737, in Bunea's dating, and moved there at once.

Orthodox Romanians pushed back. In 1744 a Serbian monk, Visarion, crossed southern Transylvania and stirred the people against the union. He was arrested on the way into Sibiu. He was questioned on 27 April 1744. Empress Maria Theresa wrote in 1746 of that impostor, the false monk (acel pseudo-monach impostor), as Bunea quotes her. Bunea adds that the movement grew far beyond one man. The people were also angry at how the bishop's requests had been met.

Bishop Klein pressed the court for his people's rights. Asked to calm the movement, he answered: „Cum vreţi să liniştesc spiritele: cu mijlóce blânde ori cu mijlóce violente?“ In a plain rendering: how do you want me to calm the people, with mild means or with force? If with mild means, he said, the rights asked for on the basis of the diplomas must be promised to us and truly given. In 1747 his supporters wrote from Daia that, if he were forced out, the Romanian people would abandon the union. Bunea says Klein himself urged that letter.

On 7 May 1751 Klein gave up his see. He did so by a formal act placed in the pope's hands.
voices: The synod of 1701 — whose own words say the Jesuit fathers of Alba Iulia opened the talks of union
Ioan Inocențiu Klein — the bishop who pressed the court for the Romanians' rights and gave up his see on 7 May 1751
Maria Theresa — who called the monk Visarion an impostor and a false monk (pseudo-monach impostor), in a letter of 1746 that Bunea quotes
Visarion Sarai — a Serbian monk whose preaching in 1744 stirred Orthodox Romanians against the union; heard here only through Bunea and the empress
entries.legacy: The church of the union lived on after 1815. Its metropolitan province, its synods and its later suppression and return are told in the next entries.
entries.peopleNote: No voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in The Romanian Greek Catholic Church: Suppression and Return, which carries it today.

entries.name: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, 1815 to 1906
entries.informalName: The church of the union under its metropolitan at Blaj
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): one study from inside the church, read in a damaged scan. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906, from the end of the earlier entry to the end of this era. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Thin. One book carries this entry: a book of 1893 by Alexandru Grama and Augustin Bunea, as the Internet Archive lists them. It was written at Blaj in answer to attacks on Metropolitan Vancea and on the union, so it argues a case. The scan is badly damaged, and the quotes keep the damage. No second study was read. The national revival, the schools at Blaj and the year 1848 are not told.
entries.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Romanian Greek Catholic Church from 1815 to 1906. It carries on the earlier entry from the union of 1698. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948.
entries.why: The church of the union had its own metropolitan at Blaj. Its synods of 1872 and 1882 set down its faith and kept its Eastern rite. In the 1890s its writers answered a claim that the union of 1698 was only a political alliance.
entries.teaser: Transylvania, 1815 to 1906. The province of Alba Iulia, its synods of 1872 and 1882, and the quarrel over the union of 1698.
entries.longDescription:
This entry carries the church of the union on from 1815. By the 1890s it was a metropolitan province with four dioceses. The metropolitan sat at Blaj.

The writers said the province stood on its own. They called it the Romanian united province of Alba Iulia. The scan prints: romângscă unită. mitropolitană de Alba-luliu.

Those writers said the province stood beside the Latin province of the Primate of Strigonium. It was not under it in any way. This is the church's own claim, made in a book of 1893.

The province held its own synods. The book says Alba Iulia was made a see again in the 1850s. Before that, only single dioceses held synods. The first provincial synod met in 1872, under Vancea. Another met in 1882.

The synod of 1872 wrote down that the Eastern rite and discipline in the church must stay untouched (să r&mână neatinse, as the scan prints it). The writers at Blaj said this was nothing new. The fathers of the synod of 1698, they said, had kept the Eastern rite and discipline for themselves and their successors.

Not everyone agreed. The Gazeta Transilvaniei attacked Vancea. So did Nicolae Densușianu. They said his synod of 1872 had harmed the law of the fathers (stricată legea strămoșăscă).

Densușianu had found the act of 1698 in 1879. The book reports that he read it as a plain political alliance of two confessions (o simplă, alianță - politică intre dóuë confesiuni, as the scan prints it) against a third, and not as a union of faith.

The writers at Blaj answered that the synod of 1872 had only written down the faith the fathers of 1698 received. So the argument turned on what the act of 1698 meant.
voices: The writers of Blaj — who answered, in 1893, that the church had always held a union of faith with Rome
Nicolae Densușianu — who found the act of 1698 in 1879 and, as the book reports him, called the union a political alliance; heard here only through his opponents
entries.legacy: The church of the union carried on past 1906. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948.
entries.peopleNote: No voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in The Romanian Greek Catholic Church: Suppression and Return, which carries it today.

entries.name: Hungarian and Transylvanian Protestantism, 1650 to 1815
entries.informalName: The Reformed and Lutheran churches of Hungary and Transylvania, from persecution to toleration
entries.statusDescription: Tier 2: one Protestant history and one Catholic study. Its window is 1650 to 1815. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. Two sources carry this entry. Bauhofer's history of 1854 is a Protestant account. The Catholic Encyclopedia article on Hungary (1910) is by A. Aldásy. Each takes one side. No source in Hungarian was read. No pastor's own account was read.
entries.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Reformed and Lutheran church of Hungary and its lands, from 1650 to 1815. The Unitarians are a different church, told to 1650.
entries.why: Catholic kings took many churches. Some pastors went to the galleys. Toleration came in 1781.
entries.teaser: Hungary and Transylvania, 1650 to 1815. The pastors sold to the galleys, the laws of 1681 and 1731, and Joseph II's toleration.
entries.longDescription:
Two sources tell this story. Bauhofer, a Protestant, writes of long suffering that ends in freedom. A Catholic work writes of a fight over churches and laws. This entry uses both.

In 1671 the bishop took the Protestant church of Kashaw, after breaking its doors. The government set up a special court at Presburg to try Protestants.

Forty-one prisoners were taken away. Only thirty entered the galleys at Naples, on 7 May. They were sold for fifty Spanish piasters apiece and chained to the benches. Ten others gave up their Protestant faith and joined the Church of Rome on 19 February 1676.

On 11 February 1676 the chaplain of the Dutch fleet came for the galley prisoners. They left their prison singing the 46th, the 114th and the 125th Psalms. Twenty-six of the thirty were still alive.

The Diet of 1681 ordered some churches returned to the Protestants. In 1687 Leopold said that by his own free favor he would keep the liberties granted in 1681. The Peace of Szathmar, signed on 10 May 1711, kept the laws of 1681 and 1687 in force.

On 21 March 1731 Charles VI gave rules the churches had long awaited. Bauhofer says their hopes were badly hurt. Private worship was allowed everywhere. Public worship was allowed only where the law of 1681 named a place.

The two churches did not always act together. In 1732 the Lutherans refused to join the Calvinists in a petition to the king. Soon after, both sent a joint statement to the court. Bauhofer reports a Count Pallfy as saying that the Protestants must have either God or the Devil for their friend. Each time their ruin seemed sure, some untoward event stopped it.

Joseph II's Edict of Toleration went to all the bishops of Hungary on 24 October 1781, in Bauhofer's account. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it was issued on 25 October. Where a hundred families could pay for it, they might build a church, a school and a manse. The churches could have neither bell nor spire, and no door onto the street.

The Diet of 1790 and 1791 gave the churches full freedom to run their own affairs, says the Catholic Encyclopedia. It counts about two million Protestants and five million Catholics in 1805.
voices: The pastors sold to the galleys at Naples — who left the boats singing the 46th, 114th and 125th Psalms on 11 February 1676
Count Pallfy — whom Bauhofer reports as saying the Protestants must have either God or the Devil for their friend
Joseph II — whose Edict of Toleration of October 1781 opened the way to Protestant churches
entries.legacy: The Reformed and Lutheran churches came out of these years with a legal footing and, after 1790, the right to manage their own affairs. The tree does not yet tell their years after 1815.
entries.peopleNote: No pastor of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: The record says the Reformed Church in Hungary and the Lutheran churches are alive today, but no dated present-day record was read. This entry ends in 1815, and the tree has no later entry for them.

entries.name: Polish and Lithuanian Catholicism Under the Partitions
entries.informalName: The Catholic Church of the partitioned Polish and Lithuanian lands
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1): the one study read covers exactly these years. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. One study carries this entry: the Catholic Encyclopedia article on Poland (1911), by E. Kolodziejczyk, a Polish Catholic. It speaks for the church and against the three powers. No pastoral letter of the time was read. Nothing from the Lithuanian press was read. Both are wanted.
entries.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Catholic Church in the partitioned Polish and Lithuanian lands from 1815 to 1906. It carries on into the entry on Polish Catholicism from 1918. The Greek Catholic church of the same lands is a different church, told in its own entry.
entries.why: After the partitions of Poland, the Catholic Church stayed with the Polish and Lithuanian peoples. Russia and Prussia tried to bend it to the state. The clergy, in one Catholic writer's words, courageously held their ground.
entries.teaser: Poland and Lithuania, 1815 to 1906. A church that stayed with a nation without a state, and the Russian and Prussian measures against it.
entries.longDescription:
After the three partitions, Russia tried to destroy the Catholic Church as well as Polish nationality, says the Catholic Encyclopedia. It dates them 1773, 1793 and 1795. This entry starts in 1815. The author is a Polish Catholic, and he speaks for the church.

In 1831 an insurrection failed. After it, the article says, Uniats were forced to give up their faith. Convents were closed, and so were churches.

Harsher measures came after 1863. A cabinet order of 1864 took the church's property and shut the convents still open. In 1867 the clergy were put under a commission at St Petersburg, with no regard for the wishes of the Apostolic See.

The measures were harshest in Lithuania. In the seven years after 1863 no more than ten priests were ordained there. Public prayers, processions and wayside crosses were forbidden.

Prussia treated its Catholic Poles no better, the article says. The clergy in Prussian Poland were put under the power of the state. Bismarck began his conflict with the Church.

After the defeat of 1863 and 1864 the clergy held their ground. In Prussia they built social and farm groups and loan offices for craftsmen and workers.

Only after the war with Japan did Russia proclaim an edict of toleration. It let those forced into the schism be reconciled with Rome.
voices: The Polish clergy — whom the article says courageously held their ground and refused to yield after 1863
E. Kolodziejczyk — the Polish Catholic author of the Catholic Encyclopedia's article on Poland, written in 1911
entries.legacy: The church that came through these years is the one told again from 1918, in the entry on Polish Catholicism under Wyszyński and John Paul II.
entries.peopleNote: No Polish or Lithuanian voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in Polish Catholicism: Wyszyński and John Paul II, which carries it today.

set.longDescription:
Zartonk — awakening — is what Armenians call their nineteenth century. A revival of language, schools, printing and civic life carried largely inside the church, because under Ottoman rule the church was the nation's legal body. Its central document is the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which seated lay delegates in a national assembly and limited what the Patriarch of Constantinople could do alone, an unusual experiment in giving a laity formal power over its own hierarchy. The century also divided the community: converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850, while an Armenian Catholic patriarchate continued alongside. And it ended in blood — the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96 killed tens of thousands and emptied whole districts.

Russia took Erivan and Etchmiadzin in 1828. Armenian volunteers helped.

In 1836 a Russian rule, the Polozhenie, tied the catholicos's rule to the state. Ormanian says it let the state meddle.

It also left the last word on bishops to the tsar. The catholicos named two men, and the tsar chose.

A Catholic work says a papal bull of 1867 caused a schism in Armenia. The bull was called Reversurus.

set.longDescription:
A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands — today's Ukraine and Belarus — was at its numerical height, holding the loyalty of most of the peasantry of the eastern Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it and also latinized it, importing Roman devotional practices into a Byzantine rite and settling its identity as something distinctly its own rather than a temporary arrangement. Then the political ground vanished: the partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 handed most of the church's people to Catherine II's Russia, which regarded the union as an amputation to be reversed, and campaigns of forced reversion from 1794 stripped it of the great majority of its parishes within two years. What survived did so in Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs raised the Greek Catholic clergy's status and paid for their education. And where the church became, over the following century, the carrier of Ukrainian national identity.

The Ruthenian church of the Carpathian lands had a union with Rome of its own, apart from the union of Brest. Nilles's heading dates the union at Uzhhorod to 1646. It dates the solemn confirmation to 1652.

In a petition of 15 January 1652, Greek-rite priests tell the pope that they were won back to Rome in the Latin church of the Uzhhorod castle, on 23 April. Their printed text names the year as 1649. Nilles notes that some read it as 1646, because the bishop of Eger who received them died in 1647.

Their earlier bishop at Mukachevo, they say, had left the union.

They joined on three terms. They would keep the Greek rite. They would have a bishop of their own choosing, confirmed by Rome. They would keep their church privileges. In their Latin, as the scan prints it: ritus graecae ecclesiae nobis servare Iice«t.

They asked Rome to confirm Peter Parthenius, the bishop they had chosen.
